title: Sarah laughs (Genesis 18:9–15)
hook: told she will bear a child at ninety, she laughs; the child will be Isaac, "he laughs"

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hachnasat orchim, bringing in guests, and an old man running in the heat. Your line was run to the guest. Who got a seat or a drink? Day forty-four.

The three strangers have eaten. And one of them asks a question guests don't usually ask: where is Sarah, your wife? In the tent, Abraham says. And the guest says: I'll come back this time next year, and Sarah your wife will have a son. Now, Sarah is standing just inside the tent door, listening. She's about ninety. Abraham is nearly a hundred. The Torah says, with real frankness, that the time for her to bear children had long passed. So she does what anyone would do hearing a stranger say something that absurd about their own body. She laughs. Not out loud. To herself. Today: the laugh behind the tent flap.
screen: `WHERE IS SARAH?` → `A SON, THIS TIME NEXT YEAR.` → `SHE LAUGHS TO HERSELF.`

segments.voice: What she says inside is honest and a little funny: after I'm worn out, am I going to have pleasure, and my husband is old too? And then God speaks to Abraham. Why did Sarah laugh, saying, shall I really bear a child, now that I'm old? Listen closely. Sarah said, my husband is old. God reports her as saying, I am old. The rabbis caught this, and loved it. The Talmud says God changed her words for the sake of peace in the home, so Abraham wouldn't be hurt. Great is peace, they said: even God shades a sentence to keep it. Then God asks the question at the heart of the story: "Is any thing too hard for the LORD?" Sarah gets scared and denies it. I didn't laugh. And the answer comes back, almost gently: "Nay; but thou didst laugh." Not a punishment. Just: you did. And it's not only Sarah. A chapter earlier, when God first promised this son, Abraham fell on his face and laughed too. Both parents laughed. So when the baby comes, a year later, they name him Yitzchak: Isaac. It means he laughs, or he will laugh. The name keeps the joke forever. And Sarah, holding him, says: "God hath made laughter for me." Everyone who hears, she says, will laugh with me. Her laugh starts out as disbelief and ends as joy, and it's the same laugh. The impossible thing became a child with a funny name.
screen: `AM I, AT MY AGE?` · `GOD CHANGES HER WORDS FOR PEACE.` · `IS ANY THING TOO HARD?` · `YITZCHAK — HE LAUGHS.` · then, large: `GOD HATH MADE LAUGHTER FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing that seems impossible to you right now. Getting well. Making up with someone. Finishing the degree. Changing a habit that's older than your kids. Say it to yourself plainly. And then let yourself smile at it, even laugh a little, the way Sarah did behind the tent. Not mocking. Just honest: this seems absurd. Hold the laugh and the hope side by side. If you pray, you can offer both. The bell holds the time.
Sarah laughs. Disbelief behind a tent door that turned into joy, and a son named Isaac, he laughs.
Your line: nothing is too hard. Today, when something looks impossible, laugh at it once, and then take one small step toward it anyway. Day forty-four.

howItsDone: Jews read Sarah's laughter in the Torah portion Vayera, and the rabbis' teaching that God changed her words for the sake of peace is often cited as a lesson about protecting peace at home.

match.prompt: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

myth: only Sarah laughed at the promise of a son
Abraham laughed first, a chapter earlier, falling on his face.
God repeated Sarah's words exactly to Abraham
she said my husband is old; God said she'd said I am old. the Talmud says it was for peace.
the name Isaac means he laughs
Yitzchak, from the Hebrew root for laughter.

fork.setup: you're Sarah, about ninety. God has just asked why you laughed, and you're scared. what do you say?
fork.reveal: she denies it, afraid, and the answer is gentle and plain: "Nay; but thou didst laugh." a year later she names her son he laughs.

original.note: Hebrew: Isaac, he laughs or he will laugh.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sarah laughed because she didn't believe God.
what it means: both parents laughed at an impossible promise, and the child was named for it: Isaac, he laughs.
what a scholar hears: Yevamot 65b and Bava Metzia 87a: God changed Sarah's words from my husband is old to I am old, for the sake of peace.

sources.quoted: Is any thing too hard for the LORD?

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 18:14, 18:15 ('Nay; but thou didst laugh') and 21:6 ('God hath made laughter for me').
Sarah's words (18:12) and God's report (18:13) are paraphrased, not quoted.
God changed her words for peace: Yevamot 65b and Bava Metzia 87a (and Rashi on 18:13). Confirm.
Sarah 'about ninety' (17:17) and Abraham 'nearly a hundred' (99 in 17:24). Confirm.
Fork: 'yes, I laughed. it's absurd.' is an invented option, not a text quotation.
